extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, comedians, humorists, critics, and students of comic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and practical methods for producing light comedy and verbal wit: identifies the fundamental mechanisms (repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference, transposition) and how they operate both in situations and in language, with examples and production guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition (comic method)
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation (a combination of circumstances) is reproduced several times in its original form within a moving series of life-like events, producing a comic 'coincidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the repeated scene as complex and as naturally introduced as possible—comic effect increases with complexity and a plausible lead‑in. Repetition may occur with the same characters in new surroundings or with different characters (e.g., masters then servants repeating a scene in a different key). Classic repetition ties to character-motivations (forces constant in direction) so the reproduction seems inevitable; modern plays may instead 'prepare' the audience so the coincidence is accepted. Examples: Moliere's Ecole des femmes, George Dandin; practical note: reconcile complexity with naturalness; use symmetrical tempi (three-stage repetition) or mirror-group structure for stronger effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion (role reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverse the situation or the roles of characters so that expectations are flipped (e.g., a prisoner lecturing a magistrate, a child teaching parents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inversion produces comedy when authority/moral or social roles recoil upon their author (the villain victim of his own villainy, the cheat cheated). It often functions even if only one side of the inverted scene is shown (the audience infers the reversed counterpart). Use it to expose topsyturvydom and to let plots punish hubris or tricksters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference of series (equivocal situations / misunderstandings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy arises when a single situation belongs at once to two independent series of events and can legitimately be interpreted in two entirely different ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct characters each embedded in their own coherent series; arrange for those series to intersect so words/actions plausibly belong to more than one series, producing equivocation. The humor depends on the audience’s awareness of both series while actors are ignorant of the other's frame. Maintain the tension by repeatedly threatening dissolution of the coincidence (near-breakdowns that are patched up), and exploit coincidence across time (past vs present) or nested sub-comedies. Example: stage-made misunderstandings, mock-heroic transpositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisation of life (absentmindedness in events/people)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy often aims to 'mechanise' life—treating living processes as repeatable, reversible, and interchangeable—turning natural continuity into a machine-like rigidity that is laughable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggerate or systematise natural absentmindedness or rigidity in action/relations to make them conspicuously mechanical. The ludicrous arises from treating living beings or events as jointed automata; this is the underpinning idea behind repetition, inversion, and interference. Note: such absentmindedness in events is exceptional and slight; the art is in amplifying it into a consistent comic system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish comic_expressed vs comic_created_by_language
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate comic that can be translated (comic expressed—dependent on situation/context) from comic that is intrinsic to the language/structure of a sentence (created by language) and often untranslatable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for language‑created comic, exploit sentence structure, word choice, and idiomatic phrase-forms rather than situational content. Recognize that many word-based jokes rely on language-specific clichés and will lose force in translation or across cultural contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit vs Comic (audience target)
rubrics_metrics.description: Witty remarks (esprit) make us smile at a third party or ourselves; the strictly comic makes us laugh at the person who utters it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to decide whether to create a retort that ridicules the interlocutor (comic) or a paradox/scene that invites broader amusement (wit). Note that many utterances straddle both categories; the writer should anticipate whether the laugh is directed at speaker, other, or audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for creating/analyzing a witticism (enlarge → categorize)
rubrics_metrics.description: To analyze or generate wit: expand a witty remark into a regular scene and identify which comic category (repetition, inversion, interference) it manifests; the witty remark is then the volatile, compressed projection of that scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reverse-engineering helps both to understand why a one-line witticism works and to create new ones: imagine the full miniature scene, map it to a comic mechanism, then compress back to a pithy line. Example: Mme. de Sévigné's 'Your chest hurts me' enlarges to a diagnosis-by-sympathy scene in Moliere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurd idea fitted into a well-established phrase-form
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic meaning is reliably obtained when an absurd idea is inserted into a ready-made, stereotyped phrase so that automatism of utterance is exposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit familiar phrase endings or idioms and subvert expectations by inserting an absurdity (e.g., 'this sword is the best day of my life'). The phrase should be recognizably conventional so the absurd insertion signals a mechanical, automatic utterance. Cultural/linguistic familiarity is necessary for effect; such jokes often resist translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literalizing metaphors / emphasising physical meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic effect occurs when a figurative expression is taken literally (fixing attention on the 'physical' meaning of a word used figuratively).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metaphors with concrete, vivid imagery and treat them as material facts (e.g., 'all the arts are brothers' → 'all the arts are sisters' or literalising running/catching metaphors into sporting images). The more concrete and unexpected the material interpretation, the stronger the comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play upon words and puns (reciprocal interference in a sentence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring two independent meanings into the same sentence so the expression legitimately reads in more than one way; the pun is a weak form (homophonic deception), while true wordplay uses one sentence to express two coherent idea-sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use polysemy and figurative/literal shifts to create parallel meanings. Be aware the pun (homophone-based) is considered the least reputable route but still a valid source of humor; stronger play uses genuine double-meaning in a single written form. The comic here often signals a momentary lapse of attention in language—exploit that apparent negligence for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion, reciprocal interference, transposition as sentence-transformation laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Three parallel laws apply to sentences: inversion (swap subject/object/roles), reciprocal interference (two meanings coexisting), and transposition (moving an idea into an incongruous stylistic 'key').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inversion is easiest but least interesting; reciprocal interference yields abundant varieties (see play-on-words); transposition is most far-reaching—treating language like repetition in action (putting ideas into a different stylistic environment so the audience supplies the natural original). Use transposition to induce an audience-supplied contrast between the expected idiom and the comic idiom actually presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition (language repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transfer ideas or expressions into a style or register that differs from their natural environment (e.g., a lofty idea rendered in low speech or vice versa), producing comedy by contrast and by audience-supplied familiarity with the original register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on the audience’s acquaintance with the 'natural' expression so they can supply it mentally when shown the transposed version alone. Transposition is comparable to repetition in action and is especially effective when the comic expression maintains internal relations of the original while existing in an incongruous setting or style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing audience acceptance vs deriving from character
rubrics_metrics.description: Two ways to make an extraordinary coincidence acceptable: have the characters’ stable dispositions/forces make the repetition/inversion inevitable (classic approach), or gradually prepare/mesmerize the audience so an unlikely event is accepted (contemporary approach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If relying on character-motivation, ensure each character represents a constant 'force' that naturally reproduces situations; if relying on audience preparation, stage the play so the spectator is conditioned to accept the coincidence (foreshadowing, gradual normalization). Choose approach based on whether you want the comic to feel character-driven or theatrical/conventional.
